cvode() and the CVODES adjoint

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-cvode.Rmd
methods-cvode.Rmd

cvode() compiles a model against SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES (\(\ge 6.0\)) of the build host for the solveODE() interface of cppODE(). Notation; arguments method, derivMode, asaCheckpoints of cvode(), gradtol of adjointControl().

Comparison with cppODE()

The two ODE backends, with the same model arguments and solveODE(). JVP: Jacobian-vector product.
cppODE() cvode()
method bdf, adams, rb4, tsit5 bdf, adams
derivMode forward, reverse, forward-reverse; deriv2 = TRUE forward, reverse
forward sensitivities dual numbers sensitivity equations, JVPs
reverse mode discrete adjoint of the computed steps continuous adjoint (CVODES ASA)
second order forward over forward, forward over reverse none
reverse options keepStore, store, adjointControl() asaCheckpoints, adjointControl(gradtol = )
libraries LAPACK; KLU optional SUNDIALS \(\ge 6.0\); KLU optional

Shared code and arguments

Shared with cppODE():

  • the code generator; \(J = \partial f / \partial x\) formed on the expression graph and emitted with linear tables and loops;
  • the arguments events, forcings, rootfunc, fixed, the returned object, and the column order, shapes (state-only, full, partial) and row names of tangent and parms;
  • the chain rule \(S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial \theta\) of Forward (2);
  • the linear solver: KLU for \(n_x \ge 8\) and structural density of \(J\) at most \(0.4\) if SuiteSparse was found at install, dense LAPACK otherwise; sparse = TRUE requires KLU;
  • PCHIP forcings, discontinuous event resets, root events at zero crossings of a user function.

Differences between the backends

Sensitivity right-hand side. CVODES integrates \[ \dot S_k = J(x, p)\, S_k + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_k}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, n_p, \tag{1} \] as one generated Jacobian-vector product of \(f\) per direction \((S_k, \partial p/\partial\theta_k)\), in double, without \(J\) and without tangent storage. cppODE() evaluates \(f\) on dual-typed state, Forward (1), for all directions in one pass.

Methods. CVODE has only the multistep families (stability) and first-order sensitivities (no deriv2 = TRUE).

Events. Generated glue outside CVODES applies the first-order Heun transport Events (2) with the firing time Events (4); CVODES re-initializes the sensitivities from it.

Adjoint sensitivity analysis

cvode(..., derivMode = "reverse") compiles the CVODES adjoint sensitivity analysis (ASA) instead of forward sensitivities and returns the $cotangent Reverse (1) of a native reverse solve, states first; the rest of the call, batch entry point included, is unchanged.

Backward problem. CVODES integrates Reverse (2) as a separate ODE [1], right-hand sides emitted as vector-Jacobian products of \(f\) (code generation) without \(J\): \[ \dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda, \qquad \dot q = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda, \tag{2} \] the second the quadrature Reverse (5) with \(q(T) = 0\). Both run from \(T\) to \(t_0\), the minus signs cancelling against the reversed limits, so \(\lambda(t_0)\) and \(q(t_0)\) are the state and parameter parts of the gradient. By default \(q\) is outside the error test: gradient entries of very different scale would stall the backward step against reltol alone. adjointControl(gradtol = g) adds it with absolute tolerance \(g\), so the step size controls the gradient error, as the checked sweep of the native mode does for discrete steps. The backward problem is a BDF solve at the tolerances and step budget of the call, with the forward linear solver (KLU for a sparse model) and the analytic Jacobian \(-J^{\mathsf T}\), formed from \(J\) in the forward pattern.

Checkpoints. CVODES stores a checkpoint every asaCheckpoints accepted steps (default \(200\), trading memory against re-integration) and recovers \(x(t)\) between checkpoints by re-integrating from the earlier one and interpolating. With interpolated states, the gradient is the derivative of no discretization performed, within \(O(\mathrm{tol})\) of both the exact gradient and the derivative of the reported value.

Jumps at observations. \(\lambda\) starts from the last cotangent row; at each earlier observation the sweep adds that row, the jump condition of Reverse (2). The problem restarts only at nonzero rows; at every output time it would reduce the method to first order at unobserved times.

Several cotangents. Cotangent columns share the checkpoints but need one backward integration each, where the native mode sweeps the stored checkpoints once per column. keepStore, store and the other adjointControl() options have no counterpart: CVODES manages checkpoints and backward step size, and a continuous adjoint has no discrete steps with errors to estimate, weight or report.

Events. CVODES cannot be re-initialized within a recorded forward run, so a model with events is integrated in stretches between jumps (a single one without events), each stretch with a CVODES memory, checkpoints, root functions and linear solver, starting from the post-jump state. The sweep runs them last to first, each from the adjoint of the later one, with the jump transpose in between: for \(x^+ = R(x^-, p, t^{*})\), \(\lambda^- = (\partial_x R)^{\mathsf T}\lambda^+\) and the gradient gains \((\partial_p R)^{\mathsf T}\lambda^+\), plus the terms of a firing time that moves with \(p\) or, for a root \(g_e(x, t, p) = 0\), with the state, \(\delta t^{*} = -(\nabla_x g_e\,\delta x + \partial_p g_e\,\delta p)/\dot g_e\), as in the adjoint of an event of the native mode. Root finding is off on a stretch before the sweep, since a root found again while CVODES recomputes the forward solution between checkpoints would label the stored data with that root time.

Restrictions. A reverse model has no forward sensitivities, and cvode() has no second order; Hessians, or gradients consistent with the returned value, need the native backend.

References

[1]
Y. Cao, S. Li, L. Petzold, and R. Serban, “Adjoint sensitivity analysis for differential-algebraic equations: The adjoint DAE system and its numerical solution,” SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing, vol. 24, no. 3, pp. 1076–1089, 2003, doi: 10.1137/S1064827501380630.
